title: The Caro-Kann Bunker
description: Meet 1.e4 with a compact centre, an active light-squared bishop and clear pawn breaks.
intro: We answer 1.e4 with the Caro-Kann and build our game around the central advance ...d5. This repertoire teaches the different structures after an exchange on d5, an advance to e5, or an early challenge with c4. White can gain space and create sharp threats, so our reliable structure still needs accurate development. Learn the pawn breaks and piece routes alongside the moves, then use the branching lines to practise recognizing White’s plans.

chapters.title: Exchange: develop around the open files
chapters.intro: The Exchange Variation removes White’s e-pawn and gives us a half-open c-file, but the positions still differ sharply according to the knight development. We bring the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 whenever White allows it. Against an early Qb3, tempo gains against the queen keep our development active. The main lesson is to coordinate the central pieces and rooks before choosing between a quiet structure and an attack on a long-castled king.

chapters.title: Advance: challenge the pawn chain
chapters.intro: White’s advance to e5 gains space and restricts our kingside knight, so we develop the light-squared bishop first and challenge the base on d4. The break ...c5 is the recurring source of counterplay, but bishop safety matters when White advances g4 or h4. Our knights often use e7, f5 or d7 rather than f6. Learn how each pawn move changes the central targets instead of treating the closed centre as a reason to wait.

chapters.title: Classical and Two Knights: the Nd7 system
chapters.intro: After exchanging on e4, we use ...Nd7 to support the development of the other knight to f6. This usually preserves our pawn structure after a knight exchange, but an early Qe2 changes which knight should move first. White can build pressure toward f7 with Bc4 and Ng5, so blocking that diagonal and gaining useful tempos matter. Our goal is active, coordinated development, with central exchanges chosen to reduce White’s initiative and free our pieces.

chapters.title: Fantasy: central pressure against f3
chapters.intro: The Fantasy Variation supports e4 with f3 and gives White a broad centre, but it also delays the kingside pieces and opens routes toward the king. We answer with ...e6 and develop the bishop to b4, where a pin can undermine the central defenders. Not every line keeps that pin, so count the defenders of d4 after each exchange. Against queenside castling, our own safe king lets us turn central pressure into queenside activity.

chapters.title: Panov: active pieces against the centre
chapters.intro: White’s early c4 challenge creates open central play and often leaves an isolated pawn on d4. We develop actively with knights on f6 and c6, then use the light-squared bishop to support or challenge the centre. A fianchetto gives our other bishop future scope, especially when the f6 knight moves. The key is combining pressure against d4 with king safety, while recognizing that pawn advances and pinned defenders can create forcing tactics.

chapters.title: Pseudo-Panov: recover the central pawn
chapters.intro: The Pseudo-Panov exchanges both of White’s central pawns and leaves a temporary pawn on d5. We develop the f6 knight against it instead of recapturing with the queen too early. Checks from b5 or a4 can change the route of our queenside knight, but development with tempo still guides the plan. Once the pawn is recovered, pressure against an isolated d4 pawn and active bishops provide clear middlegame goals without needing speculative attacks.

chapters.title: Early sidelines: occupy the centre
chapters.intro: White’s early alternatives change the development order more than our central aim: we still establish ...d5 and bring pieces out against concrete targets. Against d3, there is room for a broad centre; against Bc4, the d-pawn gains time by attacking the bishop. Early queen pressure toward f7 needs careful development and attention to pins. Learn which moves gain a useful tempo, then use that time to secure the king and coordinate the remaining pieces.
